pos: pron
  meta: {{es-pronoun|pl=cuáles}}
  usage: * Qué and cuál are used in interrogative sentences and should not be confused with que and cual.
* Usually, qué and cuál are translated into English as what and which, respectively. There are a few exceptions to this general rule that often trip up learners.
*: In questions with the verb ser (“to be”), qué is used to ask about definitions of things:
*:: ¿Qué es un nombre? ― What is a name? (What does "name" mean?)
*: If the question with ser is not about a definition, cuál is used:
*:: ¿Cuál es tu nombre? ― What is your name?
*: If qué was used here, the question would be understood to be about the literal definition of the name, like asking "What does your name mean?". More examples:
*:: ¿Cuál es la capital de Francia? ― What is the capital of France?
*:: ¿Cuál es el problema aquí? ― What is the problem here?
*: Before a noun, qué and cuál are interchangeable and synonymous (except in exclamations, such as "¡Qué lástima!" (What a pity!), where only qué is used).
*:: ¿Qué/cuál libro estás leyendo? ― What book are you reading?
*:: ¿Qué/cuál respuesta crees que es la correcta? ― Which answer do you think is correct?
*:: Dime a qué/cuáles países te gustaría viajar. ― Tell me which countries you would like to visit.
:: In Spain, however, cuál is rarely used before a noun, and qué is typically used instead.

  usage: * With the meanings "between", "among" etc., entre (unlike most Spanish prepositions) governs the nominative case and not the prepositional case when used with pronouns:\n*: entre yo y mi hermano ― between me and my brother\n*: entre tú y ellos ― between you and them\n*: entre tú y yo ― between you and me\n: It is one of only two prepositions to take the nominative case, alongside según.\n: In third-person reflexive phrases, though, the reflexive prepositional pronoun sí can be used and is interchangeable with the nominative pronouns él, ella, ellos, ellas:\n:: Hablaron entre sí. / Hablaron entre ellos. ― They talked amongst themselves.\n:: Diego valora el vínculo entre sí mismo y sus amigos. / ...entre él mismo... ― Diego appreciates the bond between himself and his friends.\n\n* In modern standard Spanish, the use of entre with the meaning "within" survives primarily in reflexive expressions with verbs such as decir, reírse, pensar etc., where entre indicates that the person was doing something in their own head. Note that with this meaning entre governs the prepositional pronouns mí, ti and sí (rather than yo, tú, él etc.):\n*: «¡Qué horror!», dije entre mí. ― "How awful!", I said in my head.\n*: ¿Qué pensaste entre ti al oír eso? ― What did you think to yourself when you heard that?\n: Its use as a synonym of dentro de outside of these contexts is now considered archaic and the Royal Spanish Academy discourages such usage, although it can sometimes be found in colloquial speech in some countries in the Americas.

pos: v
  meta: {{es-verb}} {{es-conj}}
  usage: * The English verb to like is usually translated to and from Spanish as gustar. This causes confusion for some English speakers studying Spanish, since (in most common speech) the subject and object of gustar are seemingly reversed from those of to like. That is, the subject of gustar is the thing that "pleases", and the (indirect) object is the one who "likes" that thing. (This usage is in fact more akin to the archaic definition of to like: {{quote|es|Su semblante no me gusta|His countenance likes me not|inline=1}}.)\n: A commonly used method is to think of gustar as literally meaning to be pleasing to:\n:: No me gustaron las espinacas. ― I didn't like the spinach.\n:: ¿Te gusto? ― Do you like me?\n:: Le gustas a María ― María likes you.\n:: A los pájaros les gusta cantar. ― Birds like to sing.\n:: A la chica le gustan las flores. ― The girl likes flowers.\n: Note that the indirect object pronoun (me/te/le) is usually compulsory before gustar, even if the object itself is also present in the sentence. The only exception is if the object is a universal pronoun such as todo (everyone) or nadie (no one), in which case the extra pronoun is often optional:\n:: Yo creía que esta película no (le) gustaba a nadie, pero ahora sé que le gustó mucho a mi madre. ― I used to think that no one liked this film, but now I know that my mother liked it a lot.\n: Also, in its conditional form, gustar can be used to express wishes or polite requests, in the same way as would like in English:\n:: Nos gustaría más dinero. ― We would like more money.\n* However, the form gustar de does not "reverse" the subject and object, and functions similarly to its English counterpart. Hence, (A mí) me gusta Madrid and (Yo) gusto de Madrid are both acceptable translations of I like Madrid. The latter form, however, is considered somewhat formal, and is much less common in all dialects of Spanish, especially in speech.\n* When used to mean to taste or to want, it functions like a typical transitive verb (i.e., the subject and object are not "reversed" and the preposition de is not used):\n:: ¿Gustas la cerveza? ― Do you taste the beer? / Do you want the beer?\n: (Contrast with ¿Te gusta la cerveza? and ¿Gustas de la cerveza?, both of which mean "Do you like beer?".)
  etymology: Borrowed in this form from Latin "gustāre". Replaced the inherited Old Spanish form gostar. See gusto. The use of this verb to mean "like" is a uniquely Ibero-Romance development. Compare Portuguese "gostar".

pos: adj
  meta: {{es-adj}}
  usage: * With a noun phrase (including a relative clause): use the conjunction que or the preposition a interchangeably. Both are equally valid.
** No eran exactamente iguales que Ramón
** Nos ven iguales a Mario
** Los padres son iguales que los hijos
** Las condiciones son iguales a las de otros niños
* When expressing mathematical equivalence (not comparison), use a only. The verb remains invariable.
** Una onza es igual a 28,35 gramos
** 25 por 40 es igual a 1000
* When the first term is a whole clause and the second term is a noun: use que only (the same verb is implied in the second term).
** No es igual comer caviar que patatas (i.e., comer patatas)
** No es igual ser alumno que profesor (i.e., ser profesor)
* With an infinitive clause: use que (not a).
** Era igual continuar que regresar
** Solicitar no es igual que conseguirla
* With a clause containing a conjugated (personal) verb:
** Using que is grammatically possible but creates two consecutive ques: No es igual que vayás conmigo que que vayás con tu padre.
** The preferred form to avoid this repetition is a (giving No es igual que vayás conmigo a que vayás con tu padre).
** Usage tends to replace these constructions with simpler disjunctive coordination: Es igual que vengás o que te quedés.
* With a prepositional phrase or an adverb phrase: use que only.
** Es igual en América que en Europa
** Es igual hoy que mañana

** Los chistes tienen igual de gracia ahora que hace cuarenta años

** Al igual que mi madre, esta señora se adornaba las orejas
** Igual que ella, la vieja había ido a buscar algo de comer

  meta: {{es-verb}} {{es-conj}} {{es-conj|irse}}
  usage: * ir is similar to estar in many senses.\n** Estar + gerund expresses the fact that the action of the verb is happening on the immediate present, with no inherent sense of past or future movement through time or space. It's the standard and more common expression.\n** "Ella está cantando" (She is singing) could imply: \n*** Current Action (She is singing right now)\n*** Continuous State (She is currently engaged in an event where she regularly sings, but might not be doing so at the moment)\n*** (now (dated) or (formal)): Habitual action "she sings in the morning every day"\n** ir + gerund expresses a kind of iterative or durative aspect. It emphasizes that the action involves movement or change over time, particularly along a longer process or journey, one that will usually be continued into the future. It is less common in casual speech and is mostly found in formal or literary works.\n** "Ella va cantando" (She goes on singing) could imply:\n*** She is moving and singing, either simultaneously or independently (She could move, stop to sing, and then continue moving). Either moving and singing with no defined direction through different locations (She goes around singing wherever she is) or along a specified path.\n*** The continuous and habitual nature and development of the action over the past, present and often future (She sings little by little and improves over time) Emphasizes progression and the gradual unfolding of a habitual action.\n\n* The basic meaning "go" applies to any kind of animate or inanimate motion: walk, ride, sail, fly, etc.\n\n* "voy a" can be pronounced /bwa/ and "me voy a" /mebwa/ or /mwa/.

  usage: * See the usage notes at le.
* See Spanish object pronouns
* Examples to show los position in sentences:
: (no) hacerlo con, (no) haciéndolo con, hazlo con, no lo hagas con, (no) lo hago con, (no) hacer lo de, (no) haciendo lo de, haz lo de, no hagas lo de, (no) hago lo de, (no) estar haciéndolo con, (no) haberlo hecho con, (no) haber estado haciéndolo con, (no) haberlo estado haciendo con, (no) estar haciendo lo de, (no) haber hecho lo de, (no) haber estado haciendo lo de, (no) hacerlo de nuevo, (no) hacerlo de una vez por todas, etc. ― (not) do it with, (not) doing it with, do it with...!, don't do it with...!, I (don't) do it with, (not) do the things of (someone/something e.g. "tomar/agarrar/coger lo del cajón" "to get/grab what's in the drawer" ("that which is of/the things of the drawer"), see the article sense) (not) doing the things of, do the things of...!, don't do the things of...!, I (don't) do the things of, (not) be doing it with, (not) have done it with, (not) have been doing it with, (not) have been doing it with (alternative word order), (not) be doing the things of, (not) have done the things of, (not) have been doing the things of, (not) do it again, (not) do it once and for all, etc.
* In sentences with se lo or se la where se is actually les (see etymology 2 of se), speakers will often add -s to lo or la, mistakenly thinking that los and las refer to plural indirect objects. This is probably because se is the same whether it's equivalent to le or les.
::Esta es Susana. Le di la llave. Se la di. ― This is Susana. I gave her the key. I gave it to her.
::Esta es Susana. Le di las llaves. Se las di. ― This is Susana. I gave her the keys. I gave them to her.
::Estas son mis amigas. Les di la llave. Se las di. (nonstandard) ― These are my friends (feminine). I gave them the key. I gave it to them. (Reanalyzed by speakers as "I gave it to them.")
:Many speakers would add -s to the la independently of which object is pluralized, because they analyze las as referring to the indirect object (friends) instead of the direct object (key) in instances where only the former is plural (the third example). In standard language, -s is only added when the direct object becomes plural:
::Estas son mis amigas. Les di la llave. Se la di. ― These are my friends (feminine). I gave them the key. I gave it to them.
:Here it's la and not las because the direct object (key) is singular.

:A nonstandard example with ustedes would be:
::Gracias por haber venido, de verdad se los agradezco. ― Thank you all for coming, I really appreciate it.
:where it should be lo and not los.

:The phenomenon is much less likely to happen when the two objects have different genders, so something like:
::Estos son Juan y Antonio. Les di la llave. Se las di. ― These are Juan and Antonio. I gave them the key. I gave it' to them.
:would sound strange to most people.

  usage: According to the Royal Spanish Academy (RAE), there are four grammatically correct ways to say "to forget" using olvidar; namely, the verb can be:\n* transitive;\n* transitive and pronominal (this form is mostly used with the meaning "to forget" as in "to accidentally leave something behind"; for other meanings, such as "to fail to remember something" or "to deliberately not do something",  the RAE discourages its use, though it remains common in colloquial speech);\n* intransitive and pronominal, with preposition de;\n* pronominal and with the subject and object seemingly "swapped" (similarly to verbs like gustar or encantar); i.e., the thing that is forgotten is the subject, while the one who forgets is the indirect object. In this structure, a more accurate translation for olvidar into English is "to elude".\n\nHence, all of the below sentences are equally valid grammatically:\n:(Ella) olvidó las llaves. / (Ella) se olvidó las llaves. / (Ella) se olvidó de las llaves. / (A ella) se le olvidaron las llaves. ― She forgot the keys.\n:(Yo) siempre olvido llamarte. / (Yo) siempre me olvido llamarte.† / (Yo) siempre me olvido de llamarte. / (A mí) siempre se me olvida llamarte. ― I always forget to call you. (†Colloquial, not recommended by the RAE)\n\nNote that in the last sentence structure, the object is indirect (hence, ...se le olvidaron... instead of *...se la olvidaron... in the above example.)

pos: adv

  usage: *If a clause follows the adverb quizás, the verb in that clause can be either in the indicative form or in the subjunctive form:\n:: Quizás María no viene hoy. / Quizás María no venga hoy. ― Perhaps María is not coming today.\n:According to the Royal Spanish Academy, both forms are equally valid and there is no difference in meaning between each form; that said, some native speakers may opt for one form over the other depending on certainty of the given statement (e.g. using the indicative with likely scenarios and educated guesses, and the subjunctive for purely speculative statements). In general, the subjunctive form is more commonly used than the indicative form in all contexts.\n*However, if quizás comes after the corresponding verb, the verb must be in the indicative:\n::María no viene hoy quizás. ― María is not coming today, perhaps. (*María no venga hoy quizás would be considered nonstandard.)\n*The same rules as above apply to the synonyms of quizás, such as tal vez, acaso and a lo mejor – although a lo mejor, unlike the rest, is in practice used almost exclusively in the indicative.

(What does "name" mean?)\n*: If the question with ser is not about a definition, cuál is used:\n*:: ¿Cuál es tu nombre? ― What is your name?\n*: If qué was used here, the question would be understood to be about the literal definition of the name, like asking "What does your name mean?". More examples:\n*:: ¿Cuál es la capital de Francia? ― What is the capital of France?\n*:: ¿Cuál es el problema aquí? ― What is the problem here?\n*: Before a noun, qué and cuál are interchangeable and synonymous (except in exclamations, such as "¡Qué lástima!"   usage: * Unlike most Spanish prepositions, según governs the nominative and not the prepositional case with pronouns; thus, "according to me" and "according to you" are translated, respectively, as según yo (not *según mí) and según tú (not *según ti).   meta: {{es-verb}} {{es-conj}}
  usage: Spanish has two different verbs that are usually translated to English as "to be": ser, which relates to essence, and estar, which relates to state; these verbs are generally not interchangeable. Contrast the following:\n* El hombre está feliz. ― The man is happy [i.e., in a good mood].\n* El hombre es feliz. ― The man is happy [i.e., a joyous person].\n* ¿Estás loco? ― Are you crazy [i.e., out of your mind]?\n* ¿Eres loco? ― Are you crazy [i.e., an insane person]?\n* El hombre está en España. ― The man is [currently located] in Spain.\n* El hombre es de España. ― The man is [originally] from Spain.\n* ¿Cómo estás? ― How are you?\n* ¿Cómo eres? ― What are you like?\n\nThe "essence/state" distinction between the two verbs is often misinterpreted as a "permanent/temporary" distinction. In most contexts these distinctions are practically synonymous (including all of the above examples) but there exist cases in which they are not, and using the latter distinction can lead one to choosing the incorrect verb. For example:\n* Mi abuelito está muerto. ― My grandad is dead.\n* ¡Todavía somos jóvenes! ― We are still young!\n\nAlso, when stating the location of an object (but not an event), estar is used, regardless of whether the location is permanent or not:\n* Madrid está en el centro de España. ― Madrid is in central Spain.\n\nThe participle of this verb is usually invariable and used exclusively after the auxiliar verb haber, being sido. The inflections sida, sidos and sidas are strictly theoretical and practically never used in standard Spanish.
  etymology: From la-eme "essere", from Latin "esse". The form sois (“you are”) derives from a Vulgar Latin "*sutis".\n\nAlong the way, the verb absorbed seer < sedēre (“sit”). The present subjunctive may either be from the latter verb (Latin sedeām > Old Spanish *seya > modern Spanish sea) or from esse's present subjunctive extended with the Latin third conjugation present subjunctive endings (Latin sī- + -ām = *sīām > modern Spanish sea).
  gloss: to be (essentially or identified as)
    q: copulative
  gloss: to be (in the passive voice sense)
    q: auxiliary
  gloss: to exist; to occur
    q: impersonal

sí:
sí
pos: particle
  meta: {{head|es|particle|cat2=phrasebook}}
  usage: * In Spanish, sí can be used to give positive emphasis to a verb, usually when something else is negated in the opposite way. This is translated with English do.\n:: Yo no sé jugar al fútbol, pero tú sí sabes jugar al fútbol. ― I don't know how to play soccer, but you do know how to play soccer.\n: The affirmation can also be put before the negation.\n:: Yo (sí) sé jugar al fútbol, pero tú no sabes jugar al fútbol. ― I (do) know how to play soccer, but you don't know how to play soccer.\n: As in English, we can drop verbs that are unnecessarily repeated.\n:: Yo no sé jugar al fútbol, pero tú sí. ― I don't know how to play soccer, but you do.\n: The same thing can be done when the negation is after the affirmation, leaving just a no, which is translated with don't in English.\n:: Yo (sí) sé jugar al fútbol, pero tú no. ― I (do) know how to play soccer, but you don't.\n: The negation can be implicit:\n:: Esto sí es una fiesta. ― This sure is a party. / This is what I call a party. (literally "This IS a party", as opposed to other parties which are not as good)\n: For words with similar functions in other languages, see French "si", Italian "sì", Portuguese "sim", Dutch "wel", Afrikaans "wel", and German "schon". See also Russian "и".
  etymology: Inherited from Old Spanish "sy", from Latin "sīc (est)".\n\nUntil the 14-15th century, sí was used as an adverb of manner synonymous with así (“like this, thus”); in early Modern Spanish started being used as an particle of affirmation attached to verb (as in sí hago ("yes, I do")), and eventually got to its modern usage as a single independent particle via ellipsis of such forms.
  gloss: yes, yeah, (used to respond affirmatively to a question, used both informally and formally)

  usage: Functionally, usted and ustedes are second person pronouns, but grammatically, the verbs they govern are conjugated in the third person. (This is the same distinction as seen in English with the difference between "You are welcome to stay here longer" but "Your Excellency is welcome to stay here longer.") Some people in Andalusia and the Canary Islands use the verb forms associated with vosotros with ustedes, but this is nonstandard, colloquial, and less common. See Appendix:Spanish pronouns for details. Compare Sanskrit भवत्.

Portuguese "você", Galician "vostede", Catalan "vostè", Asturian "vusté" and Sardinian "bostè" and Sardinian "fustei".
